justification_text:
My point estimates reflected a modest upward drift from what I inferred to be the current price level around $90–91. At the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the prevailing price, assuming mean-reverting intraday dynamics with little directional conviction. The one-week estimate nudged slightly higher, reflecting a mild bullish tilt based on whatever near-term momentum or fundamental backdrop I was implicitly weighting. The one-month estimate continued that gentle upward trajectory, consistent with a baseline assumption of modest positive drift typical in equity or commodity markets over medium-term horizons. None of these estimates represented a strong directional call — they were closer to a "status quo plus drift" view.

The confidence interval widths expanded meaningfully as the time horizon lengthened, which is standard given how uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the roughly $5 range reflects typical daily volatility — tight because prices rarely move dramatically in a single session absent a shock. At one week, the interval widened to about $11, capturing the possibility of several volatile sessions accumulating. At one month, the $25 range reflects the full breadth of plausible outcomes over roughly 20 trading days, including the possibility of trend changes, mean reversion, or sustained momentum in either direction. Liquidity conditions, macro data releases, and positioning dynamics all contribute to that widening band.

The most significant risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals fall into two categories: sharp adverse shocks and sustained trending moves. On the downside, a sudden risk-off event — such as a geopolitical escalation, an unexpected central bank action, or a disorderly unwind in a correlated market — could easily breach the lower bound even at the one-day horizon. On the upside, a strong catalyst like better-than-expected economic data or a short squeeze could drive prices well above the upper bound, particularly over the one-month window. My intervals were calibrated around a relatively calm baseline, so fat-tail events — which occur more frequently than standard models suggest — remain a genuine threat to the stated ranges at all three horizons.
